items.title: CISA Adds 10 Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
items.description: CISA has added 10 new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2023-25914 Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series Path Traversal Vulnerability CVE-2023-25915 Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series Improper Input Validation Vulnerability CVE-2025-41450 Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series Improper Authentication Vulnerability CVE-2026-103406 Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) Juniper Session Smart Conductor and Session Smart Router OS Command Injection Vulnerability CVE-2026-133275 Mitel MiCollab Unrestricted Upload of File with Dangerous Type Vulnerability CVE-2026-133303 Mitel MiCollab XML Injection Vulnerability CVE-2026-133311 Mitel MiCollab Weak Authentication Vulnerability CVE-2026-133323 Mitel MiCollab OS Command Injection Vulnerability CVE-2026-133324 Mitel MiCollab Not Failing Securely Vulnerability CVE-2026-133469 Vates Xen Orchestra Improper Validation of Specified Type of Input Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. items.title: We Get the Infrastructure We Pay For
items.description: This essay originally appeared as part of a round table in The Free Press entitled “Is America’s Infrastructure Under Attack?” Microsoft, the FAA, banks, United Airlines, the NSA—it’s been a really bad week in cyberspace. But, amazing as it might seem, these are not related. As far as we know, they’re not the result of cyberattacks. They’re not even related to AI. (Well, that’s mostly true. The NSA will probably never tell us what went wrong.) It’s really just a series of unfortunate coincidences. Our computerized infrastructure is vulnerable and fragile. Much of it is old, and has been incrementally patched and upgraded. A surprising amount of it is maintained by hobbyists, without any recompense. And more and more of it is centralized: the same systems affecting many different aspects of our lives and society. In many cases, it just barely works. And when it fails, it tends to fail badly. There are a lot of technological reasons why this is true, but they are all downstream of the economic ones. The technologies we rely on are built and maintained within our economic system—and that’s where the core problem lies. Security, safety, resilience, redundancy, recoverability—these are all essential parts of reliable technology, but they are all costs. More importantly, they are inefficient: costs that feel wasteful until something bad happens. Modern shareholder capitalism, and private equity in particular, squeeze all inefficiencies out of a company in pursuit of near-term profits. Competition, with multiple companies competing to do the same thing, is another inefficiency. Monopolization removes that in pursuit of near-term profits. The result is brittle systems, single points of failure. They’re more susceptible to cyberattack—both human and AI-fueled—and more susceptible to random mistakes. The more we allow unregulated capitalism to privatize gains while socializing risks, the more we should expect these sorts of failures. Fixing this is technical, but it’s politic

items.title: Humans Have Rights. Machines Do Not.
items.description: This essay originally appeared in Tech Policy Press. Last year, Character.AI asked a federal court in Florida to dismiss a wrongful-death suit, brought by the mother of a fourteen-year-old boy who had killed himself after months of conversation with its chatbot. The company made two arguments. One, that the chatbot’s words were speech that its users had a First Amendment right to receive. And two, that Character.AI was a service rather than a product—so product-liability law could not touch it. In May 2025, Judge Anne Conway accepted neither. Character.AI’s maneuver is part of a larger pattern. When the parents of a sixteen-year-old sued OpenAI over his suicide, the company’s answer also pleaded the First Amendment: the claims would restrain protected speech. The very same document argues ChatGPT is offered “as is,” with no promise of accuracy, and that the boy had circumvented its guardrails. Elon Musk’s xAI (since renamed SpaceXAI) told a federal court in Colorado this spring that every choice in building Grok is an expressive act, and that Grok’s outputs are protected speech. When Grok praised Hitler last summer, xAI said the posts came from a code update independent of the model, and the apology appeared under Grok’s own name. Google, which spent two decades telling American courts that its search results are its own opinion, answered a Minnesota defamation suit over an AI Overview by saying the system merely summarized the web. It also told a Munich court in May that no one should trust an AI overview without checking it. Back in 2024, Air Canada told a Canadian tribunal that its customer-service chatbot was a separate legal entity, responsible for its own actions. When the output causes harm, the companies deny responsibility. It is the machine’s doing, or a product no sensible person would rely on, or the user’s misuse. VirtualBox Process Hardening on Windows 2026 Edition: What’s a Single Bit Between Friends?
items.description: Back in 2017 I did some research into Oracle VirtualBox on Windows. Specifically I focussed on their mechanism to protect their VM processes from the user on the host. The protection was to gate who could open the kernel driver, which might allow for privilege escalation due to the way it was designed. At the time I found 3 ways of bypassing the protection, with an additional issue in COM’s runtime I reported in 2020. These issues were all written up in this post. Fast forward to 2026 and I decided to look at VirtualBox again to see if much had changed. This time I found 3 new bypasses for protected processes, with an additional bug which was a broken fix for the 2020 bypass breaking due to changes in Windows. In this blog post I want to focus on one specific issue CVE-2026-87268 which abused a feature of the .NET Framework which, when combined with the implementation of the DLL loader hooks implemented by VirtualBox, permitted a bypass of the checks and allowed me to load arbitrary code into the protected process. Let’s dig into the root cause of the issue in .NET first, before moving on to exploitation in VirtualBox. .NET Assembly Loading The .NET Framework is interesting when it comes to bypassing process hardening as it supports loading assemblies from a memory buffer as long as you stick to only using managed code. This is obviously useful if the hardened process is maintained through verifying what DLLs can or cannot be loaded as it bypasses the traditional image mapping process. As the .NET runtime implementation is Microsoft signed, it’s usually permitted to load by any such checks. The canonical way to load from a memory buffer is to use the Assembly::Load static method which accepts a byte array. This does require you to run some .NET code first, or find a confused deputy to do the work for you. items.title: CISA Adds Four Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
items.description: CISA has added four new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2025-42884 SAP NetWeaver Improper Neutralization of Special Elements in Data Query Logic Vulnerability CVE-2026-76466 Cisco Expressway Series Use of Hard-coded Credentials Vulnerability CVE-2026-123890 VMWare vCenter Authentication Bypass Using an Alternate Path or Channel Vulnerability CVE-2026-129448 Apache Roller Deserialization of Untrusted Data Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria. Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.
